newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-Peseta strength exerts pressure to cut rates.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Peseta strength exerts pressure to cut rates.

text.p: A powering peseta has heightened expectations that the Bank of Spain could soon sanction its first interest rate cut of the year to help restrain the currency, traders said on Monday.

After months of straining at the bit, the peseta broke free on Friday and stormed through the 84.00 per mark barrier to trade at levels not seen since last May after the Bank of Spain released its firm grip and refrained from intervening.
The peseta strengthened further on Monday to trade as low as 83.35, compared with late Friday's levels of 83.47. By midday, it had stabilised to 83.40 per mark.
Some traders have interpreted the central bank's absence from the currency market as a sign that it may now turn to other means to control the currency, namely interest rates.
"The Bank of Spain could resort to other instruments now to hold back the peseta, with (a cut in) the repo rate being an obvious choice," said one trader.
A handful of analysts said the Bank of Spain could choose its regular repurchase auction on Thursday to trim its key money rate from 6.25 percent.
"It's 50/50 at the moment for this Thursday but a stronger peseta certainly means there is a higher chance of a small cut of perhaps 25 basis points," said one analyst.
However, the dominant feeling amongst analysts was that inflation remained the key determinant for future rate cuts as the single European currency approaches.

"Inflation is more important than the peseta for the Bank of Spain as inflation is one of the Maastricht criteria and if it doesn't deliver the goods on the inflation front we are not going to make it," said Alfredo Urrutia, chief economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.

The central bank is keen to wait for evidence that inflation has fallen below three percent before sanctioning further cuts, many analysts said. The consumer price index was up 3.2 percent year-on-year in November.
They added that the market was discounting aggressive interest rate cuts this year and it was this that was powering the peseta rather than the reverse.

In recent months, the peseta has remained at the mercy of the central bank which is thought to be keen to hold the currency in the 84.00 to 85.00 per mark band in the run up to a single European currency.

Considerable inflows into Spain's bond and equity markets, sparked partly by the belief that Spain will be in the first wave to join Europe's monetary union (EMU), have exerted signficant pressure on the peseta to appreciate.
Some dealers and analysts said disapproving looks from EU partners who may desire a stronger peseta and billowing currency reserves may be taking their toll on the central bank.
Others said the Bank of Spain had held back on intervening, hoping the market would find its feet around 84.00 per mark.
"The Bank of Spain has finally decided not to play too aggressively and let the market come to its own conclusion that the appreciation is a bit over the top," said Urrutia.
